Oura can help close meaningful care-engagement gaps for members with known high-cost health needs

Employer benefits are often built around enrollment, episodes of care, or discrete outreach, leaving gaps for members whose engagement does not persist.

Left of the Gap
Wellness Engagement
  • Passive tracking, no accountability
  • Generic content for everyone
  • No path to clinical care

e.g., meditation and fitness apps, generic sleep content, step challenges

Right of the Gap
High-Touch Clinical Care and Care Management
  • Reactive, not preventive
  • Expensive, nurse- or clinician-led
  • Reserved for the diagnosed only

e.g., Omada for diabetes/HTN/weight, CPAP and sleep programs, GLP-1 support, Accolade/Personify navigation, virtual care and plan care management

OURA
Fills the space between
Unmanaged Middle

An Oura-powered engagement layer for members with known health needs who are not enrolled, are disengaging, or are too low-acuity for ongoing human outreach.

e.g., Inconsistent CPAP use (sleep)·Unmanaged hypertension·Stopped diabetes prevention program·At-risk or stopped GLP-1

What Oura Offers
High Daily Engagement

Built into members’ existing daily routine.

Continuous Biometric Signals

Longitudinal view of sleep, recovery, and behavior.

Personalized AI Guidance

Turns personal data into a clear next step and customized nudge.

Smart Escalation

Uses low-cost AI triage and on-demand telehealth before higher-touch care.

Path to scale a recurring employer revenue pool: PMPM activation revenue, plus ring and membership economics, can reach ~$300M annually at $5 PEPM across 5M members.

Creates a no-regret path into clinical care: Oura owns engagement around existing care while partners retain clinical staff, licensure, networks, and treatment accountability, building Oura’s proof before taking on more clinical responsibility.

Targets white space: Condition platforms focus on enrolled members, while navigators prioritize higher-value episodes. Oura can re-engage employees that are unsupported, initially complementing incumbents and ultimately competing for condition-specific and navigation spend.

Focus

Helping employees find and reach the right care when a need arises — an established, maturing category at ~$4.5B today, growing ~7% annually as large, self-funded employers manage more complex medical spend.

Focus

Most programs focus on people who already have a diagnosis, such as diabetes, hypertension, weight, or musculoskeletal conditions. Their core challenge is getting those members to enroll and stay engaged.

How they make money

The buying model is bifurcated: national carriers embed basic navigation into ASO/TPA fees, while employers separately buy independent platforms when they need a stronger member experience, more clinical guidance, or measurable cost reduction.

How they make money

Disease-management programs are typically sold condition by condition, with employers paying a monthly fee for eligible or enrolled members and expecting measurable outcomes.

Trend

The category is converging with care delivery and condition support — leading platforms increasingly pair navigation with virtual care and condition programs, making navigation the control point for directing members to the right benefit and site of care.

Trend

AI and continuous data can shift the model from coaching known patients to identifying and activating risk earlier.

Care navigation

Reducing preventable emergency department and urgent care visits, replacing in-person visits (e.g., behavioral health) with digital visits, and steering towards lower-cost facilities.

Slows the growth of the ~$5.3K average cost carried by the movable-middle employee. The same capability can slow cost growth across the other tiers on the prior slide as well.

Care gap activation

Prevents the ~$5.3K employee from progressing into the ~$22K or ~$67K employee.

Care Navigation: For an In-the-Moment Need

One moment of guidance can save the employer up to $2,036 in ED visits

Healthspan Balance Seeker · Mid-life parent/caregiver · Pragmatic about her health

“I don’t want to overreact, but I also don’t have time to guess wrong about my health.”

Elaine wakes at 2 a.m. with a sudden fever, chills and a pounding headache. With family and work depending on her, she wants a quick, reliable answer on what to do next.

Without Oura

Care Gap Closure: For a Known Condition

One early nudge stops a small gap from compounding into years of cost

Mark, 47

Younger Adult Managing a Condition · Managing hypertension while balancing work and everyday life

“I want to know what’s changing between visits. Staying consistent when life gets busy is the hard part.”

Mark is managing hypertension, but most of his life happens between clinical visits. Small changes in sleep, stress, activity and adherence can compound before either Mark or his care team sees the full picture.

Without Oura

01

Routine Slips

A demanding week throws Mark off routine, and he misses his blood-pressure medication a few times.

02

No Immediate Feedback

He feels largely normal, with little indication that his hypertension may be becoming less controlled.

03

Control Deteriorates

Missed medication, stress and disrupted sleep contribute to worsening blood-pressure control.

04

Compounding Cost

What started as one skipped prescription turns into years of rising cost for Mark.

Cost trajectory keeps climbing

With Oura

01

A Subtle Signal

A shift in Mark’s sleep and recovery signal hints that something’s off.

02

A Gentle Check-In

Oura uses that same signal to check in with him directly.

03

A Timely Nudge

A simple nudge reminds Mark to take his medication, right when it matters.

04

The Loop Reopens

Oura keeps watching, so if Mark slips again, the loop reopens right away.

$1,441 avg. annual savings

HIGH

HIGH

PAP adherence is associated with lower utilization and healthcare costs (claims study).

GLP-1 persistence and behavior support

20.4% discontinue by month 3; 32.0% by month 12.

Obesity (Gasoyan et al., 2025) ↗
MED–HIGH

Oura does not prove medication use, but daily sleep, recovery, activity, and engagement can support the behavior change around treatment.

MED–HIGH

The target is members receiving GLP-1s through a PCP, PBM, or cash-pay path without wraparound support, plus members who disengage from an existing program. There is no whitespace where an employer already buys Omada-style GLP-1 management unless Oura improves re-engagement.

HIGH

Drug spend is immediate, and persistence determines whether that spend generates durable benefit.

Only 9.5% of eligible employees enrolled in one employer DPP; nationally, only 22% attended ≥10 months.

Enrollment: PubMed ↗Attendance: Herman et al., 2023 ↗
HIGH

Oura can reinforce the sleep, activity, and recovery behaviors DPPs require.

HIGH

DPP vendors have the intervention, but opt-in enrollment and retention remain low, particularly as coaching cadence declines. Navigation can refer, but referral alone has not closed the gap.

MED–HIGH

Prevented or delayed diabetes has a real employer ROI, with CDC tools specifically estimating health benefit and ROI for employer DPP coverage (CDC).

Menopause symptom-to-care activation and follow-through

Roughly 80% of women experience bothersome menopausal symptoms affecting quality of life and work.

The Menopause Society ↗
MED–HIGH

Temperature, sleep, recovery, and cycle context are unusually relevant to the member experience.

MED–HIGH

Midi, Maven, Ovia, and others provide menopause care, while Accolade can route. The potential gap is members who do not recognize a treatable need, do not use the available service, or do not sustain symptom-management actions.

MED

Strongest value is productivity, presenteeism, and retention. Workplace interventions have improved work-related outcomes, but the hard-dollar evidence is less mature (review).

Appendix

What has to hold true for this strategy to scale beyond the wedge

−

Headwinds

  • Incremental demand is unproven. The model assumes employer sponsorship drives new Ring purchases. That is a hypothesis, not yet validated with consumer research or an employer pilot.
  • Hardware economics do not scale as is. Potential partners have said the Ring’s hardware cost is too high for a software-only PMPM model. Lower-cost hardware is a longer-term unlock.
  • The wedge and the scale case are different problems. Winning an initial employer wedge is not the same as building the go-to-market motion and capabilities needed for a broader employer-wide promise.
  • Capabilities still need to be built. Care navigation and condition-management capabilities must be built, bought, or partnered for. The timeline may run longer than the window of opportunity.
  • Oura enters a market with entrenched incumbents. Accolade, Included Health, Omada, and others already hold employer relationships. Oura needs a clear point of view on how it coexists with them.
+

Tailwinds

  • Employer cost pressure is rising. Mercer projects 6.7% employer health-benefit cost growth in 2026, creating urgency for new savings levers.
  • GLP-1 and specialty drug costs are surging. This is a fresh source of demand for navigation-led steering that Oura’s signals can support.
  • AI is lowering the cost to serve. Continuous, low-cost signal can make navigation economics work at a broader population than incumbents can profitably reach today.
  • Partnership appetite already exists. Recent conversations with employer navigation players show real interest in a better-together model pairing their go-to-market with Oura’s engagement.
  • Continuous engagement is a real differentiator. No existing navigation or condition-management competitor combines daily biometric signal with a hardware relationship.
The near-term wedge is credible. The open questions are whether hardware economics, capability build-out, and incremental demand can be proven fast enough to scale beyond it.
